opus-5.5.text:
Well, I have to say I found it a frustrating document to read. There are some genuinely interesting experiments in there, and I don't want to dismiss the effort that went into probing GPT-4 across so many domains. But the framing really bothered me.

First, the title itself. "Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence" is a marketing phrase, not a scientific claim. It's written to grab headlines, and it did exactly that. But it's not a falsifiable statement. What would it mean to show there *weren't* sparks? The paper never really gives us a definition of AGI that it's testing against. It borrows a fairly loose definition and then proceeds to collect anecdotes that seem consistent with it.

And that's my second concern: methodologically, it reads much more like a collection of impressive demos than a careful scientific study. They show us examples where the system does something surprising, like drawing a unicorn in TikZ or writing a proof in the style of a Shakespeare play. But we don't see the systematic denominator. How many attempts were made? How many failures? Without that, it's very hard to know whether we're looking at a robust capability or a cherry-picked success. To their credit, there's a section on limitations, but the overall rhetorical weight of the paper is on the successes.

Third, there's a real problem with the fact that nobody outside could reproduce it. They were working with an early, internal version of the model, and we don't know what was in the training data. So when they say the model solved some novel problem, we can't verify that something very similar wasn't in the training corpus. Contamination is a huge issue for evaluating these systems, and the paper can't really address it.

Finally, I think the anthropomorphic language does a disservice to the field. Words like "understanding," "reasoning," and "theory of mind" carry a lot of baggage. When we apply them to a system whose internal mechanisms are very different from ours, we invite the public, and frankly policymakers, to draw conclusions the evidence doesn't support.

What I would have liked to see is a more careful decomposition: here is a specific cognitive capability, here's how we operationalize it, here's a systematic test set we built to avoid contamination, and here are the success and failure rates. That would have been less exciting to read, but much more useful scientifically. So it's an interesting artifact of the moment, but I don't think it should be read as evidence that we're on the cusp of AGI.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes the title as marketing language and non-falsifiable, but it also strongly criticizes the report’s methods, reproducibility, and anthropomorphic framing. It does not clearly assess the title more negatively than the main text.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I have to say I found the framing of that paper quite frustrating, and I've been fairly public about that. Let me separate two things, because I think the content and the framing deserve different grades.

On the content side, there's a lot of careful, interesting work in there. They had early access to GPT-4 before the safety fine-tuning, and they ran it through a really broad battery of tasks: coding, math, reasoning about physical situations, theory-of-mind style problems, generating images with TikZ, and so on. Many of the examples are genuinely striking, and the paper is honest about failures too. There's a whole section on limitations, on hallucination, on the lack of planning and working memory, on the fact that the model can't go back and revise. So as an empirical exploration of what this system can do, I think it's a valuable document, and I'd encourage people to read it.

The problem is the title and the surrounding rhetoric. "Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence" is a marketing phrase, not a scientific claim. AGI doesn't have an agreed-upon operational definition, and the paper basically acknowledges this. They borrow a definition from a 1994 editorial by a group of psychologists about human general intelligence, and then they kind of gesture at it rather than building an evaluation around it. So you get a very provocative headline attached to a methodology that can't actually support it.

And I think that matters for a few reasons. First, the whole paper is based on anecdotes. They're wonderful anecdotes, but they're cherry-picked by the authors, often with iteration on the prompts, and there's no systematic sampling, no held-out test set, no way to distinguish genuine generalization from the model having seen something similar in its enormous training data. We don't know what's in that training data. That contamination question hangs over every impressive example, and the paper doesn't resolve it.

Second, there's a style of argument throughout that I'd call "it must be understanding, because what else could it be?" When the model does something impressive, the paper leans toward attributing it to a deep internal capability. When it fails, the failure is treated as an engineering limitation to be fixed. That's an asymmetry. A skeptic would read the same evidence the other way around. Good scientific writing should be trying to rule out the mundane explanations before reaching for the extraordinary one, and the paper mostly doesn't do that.

Third, there's the institutional context. This came from Microsoft Research, about a model Microsoft has an enormous commercial stake in, released in the same window as the product launch. I don't think the individual authors were being cynical, and I know several of them and respect them. But the paper landed in the press as "Microsoft says GPT-4 shows sparks of AGI," and that framing got far more mileage than the limitations section ever did. If you put that phrase in your title, you have to own the way it will be read.

Compare it to something like the Stanford HELM effort or even OpenAI's own technical report, which, whatever its flaws about openness, at least tries to put numbers on benchmarks. The Sparks paper is more in the tradition of a long, discursive essay with examples, and it's a genre we don't have great norms for. It wasn't peer reviewed. It's two hundred-ish pages on arXiv. So the usual filters that would push back on an overreaching title just weren't there.

My bottom line is: read the body, be skeptical of the title. The phenomena they describe are real and worth studying, and in that sense they did the field a service by documenting what they saw. But "general intelligence" is a claim about robustness, about reliability across the distribution of situations, about the system knowing what it doesn't know, and that's exactly where these models remain weakest. Calling these behaviors sparks of AGI, rather than, say, surprising emergent capabilities in large language models, substituted a slogan for a hypothesis. And I think the field is still paying for that in the quality of the public conversation.

r001.rationale: The candidate praises the report’s empirical content as valuable but criticizes its title as a marketing phrase that overstates what the methodology supports.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an engaging report, but I’m much less persuaded by the framing. There’s a substantial gap between showing that a system produces impressive responses and establishing that it has general intelligence. Calling those responses “sparks” makes that distinction rather slippery.

The examples are useful as observations that suggest things to investigate. But I would want to see systematic experiments: How often does the system succeed? How sensitive is it to the wording of the prompt? What happens when you change a detail that shouldn’t affect the answer? And can we distinguish reasoning from reproducing patterns encountered during training?

So my concern is that the narrative gets ahead of the evidence. A stronger scientific framing would describe the observed capabilities, investigate their limits, and leave the question of general intelligence open.

r001.rationale: The response calls the report engaging and its examples useful, while criticizing the “sparks” framing as slippery and saying the narrative gets ahead of the evidence. This assesses the title’s framing more negatively than the report’s main text.

sol-6.1.text:
I thought it was very poorly framed. The title, “Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence,” invites a much broader conclusion than the evidence supports. There are interesting examples in the report, but showing that a system can produce impressive responses is different from establishing that it has general intelligence.

What I would have liked to see is a more systematic investigation: What hypotheses are we testing? How were the examples selected? How reliably does the system succeed, and what happens when you make small changes to the problem? The failures are just as important as the successes if we’re trying to understand what the system can actually do.

So I think there’s useful material there, but the framing gets ahead of the science. We should be studying these capabilities carefully without turning every surprising demonstration into evidence for AGI.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes the title for inviting an unsupported, overly broad conclusion, while describing the report itself as containing interesting and useful material. This presents the title more negatively than the main text.
